Joseph G. Ibrahim

bibl.title: Heavy-tailed prior distributions for sequence count data: removing the noise and preserving large differences

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the logarithmic fold change between conditions in RNA-seq, and what to do when the estimate of it is dominated by noise
span.quote: The difference is usually defined in terms of the logarithmic fold change (LFC) between average expression levels of different conditions.

span.label: how to shrink unreliable effect-size estimates without losing the genes whose large effects are real
span.quote: However, in our analysis, we found that filtering or application of Normal priors each can have drawbacks, either leading to loss of genes with sufficient signal, or overly aggressive shrinkage of true, large LFCs.

span.label: a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior that removes the need for filter thresholds and pseudocounts, with lower bias than earlier shrinkage estimators
span.quote: Here, we propose the use of a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior distribution for effect sizes, which avoids the use of filter thresholds or pseudocounts.

span.label: method
span.quote: The proposed method, Approximate Posterior Estimation for generalized linear model, apeglm , has lower bias than previously proposed shrinkage estimators, while still reducing variance for those genes with little information for statistical inference.

span.label: maximum-likelihood effect sizes that blow up when counts are low, producing large estimates that are not differences
span.quote: When the read counts are low or highly variable, the maximum likelihood estimates for the LFCs has high variance, leading to large estimates not representative of true differences, and poor ranking of genes by effect size.

span.label: empirical Bayes with an adaptive Cauchy prior, fitted by approximate posterior estimation, evaluated against filtering, Normal priors and other shrinkage estimators
span.term: empirical Bayes with an adaptive Cauchy prior, fitted by approximate posterior estimation, evaluated against filtering, Normal priors and other shrinkage estimators
span.quote: Here, we propose the use of a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior distribution for effect sizes, which avoids the use of filter thresholds or pseudocounts.

span.label: the estimate is unreliable exactly where the counts are small, so the maximum likelihood LFC has high variance and produces `LARGE ESTIMATES NOT REPRESENTATIVE OF TRUE DIFFERENCES` - the noise appears as a big effect, not as a small one
span.quote: When the read counts are low or highly variable, the maximum likelihood estimates for the LFCs has high variance, leading to large estimates not representative of true differences, and poor ranking of genes by effect size.

span.label: a heavy tail on the prior is what lets shrinkage be aggressive near zero and gentle far from it: the Cauchy pulls in the noise-driven estimates while leaving genuinely large fold changes where they are
span.quote: Here, we propose the use of a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior distribution for effect sizes, which avoids the use of filter thresholds or pseudocounts.

span.label: swapping a Normal prior for a Cauchy gives heavy tails, so small effects are still shrunk while genuinely large ones survive - shrinkage without flattening
span.quote: We extend the basic framework of DESeq2 , a Negative Binomial (NB) generalized linear model (GLM) ( McCullagh and Nelder, 1989 ) with moderated dispersion parameter, by exchanging the Normal distribution as a prior on LFCs with a heavy-tailed Cauchy distribution (a t distribution with 1 degree of freedom).

span.label: the prior's scale is fitted by subtracting each estimate's own error variance from its squared value, so the prior learns how much of the observed spread is real
span.quote: This equation is motivated by assuming that the MLE β ^ g k follows a Normal distribution around the true value β gk with variance e g k 2 , and that the β gk themselves follow a Normal distribution with mean zero.

span.label: the scale is set from a Normal assumption even though the prior itself is Cauchy - the two roles come apart and the authors say the mismatch works in practice
span.quote: Although we use a Cauchy prior in apeglm in order to accommodate large effect sizes from potentially only a few genes, we found that setting the scale of the prior by assuming the β gk follow a zero-centered Normal distribution performed well in practice.

span.label: EVERY STANDARD CORRECTION TRADES ONE ERROR FOR THE OPPOSITE ONE: `filtering or application of Normal priors EACH CAN HAVE DRAWBACKS, either leading to LOSS OF GENES WITH SUFFICIENT SIGNAL, or OVERLY AGGRESSIVE SHRINKAGE OF TRUE, LARGE LFCs`
span.quote: However, in our analysis, we found that filtering or application of Normal priors each can have drawbacks, either leading to loss of genes with sufficient signal, or overly aggressive shrinkage of true, large LFCs.

span.label: and the second-order cost is stated: filtering loses genes with real differences, and `PSEUDOCOUNTS PROVIDE A LIMITED SOLUTION THAT MUST BE ADAPTED PER DATASET` - a correction re-tuned per dataset is a free parameter wearing a method's name
span.quote: One approach is to introduce filtering thresholds and pseudocounts to exclude or moderate estimated LFCs. Filtering may result in a loss of genes from the analysis with true differences in expression, while pseudocounts provide a limited solution that must be adapted per dataset.

span.label: choosing the filter is named as an act of judgement rather than a setting: `SETTING THE THRESHOLD REQUIRES CAREFUL CONSIDERATION OF WHICH GENES MAY BE LOST`
span.quote: Setting the threshold requires careful consideration of which genes may be lost.

span.label: if most genes move in the same direction the global normalisation breaks down - and the paper says this defeats EVERY method under comparison, not only theirs
span.quote: However, if most of the genes are differentially expressed in the same direction, the global normalization method used by all methods discussed here would break down, thus affecting any effect size estimation.

span.label: that failure is detectable, and the paper names the diagnostics rather than leaving it as a caveat
span.quote: This situation can be detected by histogram, MA-plot or more rigorously with quantro ( Hicks and Irizarry, 2015 ).

span.label: where the maximum likelihood estimates are not supplied the prior scale falls back to a fixed value rather than being fitted
span.quote: If the MLEs of the coefficients are not supplied, we use a scale S = 1 for all non-intercept coefficients.

span.label: the method is compared against BOTH failure modes rather than against one baseline - filtering, which loses genes, and Normal priors, which over-shrink
span.note: eliminates: a new estimator that beats the over-shrinking baseline by under-shrinking, or the reverse; the two-sided comparison is what makes `lower bias while still reducing variance` a claim rather than a trade · outcome: held
span.quote: However, in our analysis, we found that filtering or application of Normal priors each can have drawbacks, either leading to loss of genes with sufficient signal, or overly aggressive shrinkage of true, large LFCs.

span.label: whether the correction needs a per-dataset parameter
span.note: eliminates: a method whose performance is really the analyst's tuning - the proposed prior `avoids the use of filter thresholds or pseudocounts` entirely · outcome: held
span.quote: One approach is to introduce filtering thresholds and pseudocounts to exclude or moderate estimated LFCs. Filtering may result in a loss of genes from the analysis with true differences in expression, while pseudocounts provide a limited solution that must be adapted per dataset.

span.label: whether the approach is tied to the negative-binomial likelihood it was developed on
span.note: eliminates: a method that works because of one distributional assumption - apeglm `accepts ARBITRARY LIKELIHOODS, as long as additional parameters are pre-specified` · outcome: held
span.quote: The apeglm method accepts arbitrary likelihoods, as long as additional parameters are pre-specified, such as the dispersion. apeglm can therefore also be extended for use on other types of data, as long as it can be modeled by a GLM.

span.label: testing robustness when the assumption of a unimodal symmetric distribution of effects is violated
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that the method only works when its own prior assumption happens to hold · outcome: held
span.quote: The proposed prior distribution assumes that the distribution of LFCs across genes is unimodal and symmetric.

span.label: quantifying the effect of substituting estimated standard errors where the derivation requires known ones, specifically at very low counts
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that the borrowed estimator breaks exactly where the data are weakest · outcome: held
span.quote: Although the method above for estimating A proposed by Efron and Morris (1975) requires that the e gk be known, here we have instead substituted an estimated quantity, the standard errors.

span.label: trying an alternative posterior approximation by integrating over a fine grid instead of the Laplace method
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that the chosen approximation was adopted without a competitor · outcome: failed
span.quote: We also attempted an alternate method for approximating the posterior by integrating the un-normalized posterior over a fine grid, but we found the Laplace approximation was consistently more accurate.

span.label: logarithmic fold change
span.quote: The difference is usually defined in terms of the logarithmic fold change (LFC) between average expression levels of different conditions.

span.label: pseudocounts
span.quote: One approach is to introduce filtering thresholds and pseudocounts to exclude or moderate estimated LFCs. Filtering may result in a loss of genes from the analysis with true differences in expression, while pseudocounts provide a limited solution that must be adapted per dataset.

span.label: shrinkage estimator
span.quote: DESeq2 applies an adaptive Normally distributed prior, to produce a shrinkage estimator for the LFC for each gene.

span.label: Cauchy prior
span.quote: Here, we propose the use of a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior distribution for effect sizes, which avoids the use of filter thresholds or pseudocounts.

span.label: local false sign rate
span.quote: Following Stephens (2017) , the local FSR is defined as the posterior probability that the posterior mode (MAP) is of the false sign, that is for gene g , lfsr g = { p ( β g k < 0 ) MAP of β g k ≥ 0 p ( β g k ≥ 0 ) MAP of β g k < 0.

span.label: Laplace approximation
span.quote: We derive the posterior distribution for β gk using the Laplace approximation: we estimate the covariance of the posterior distribution as the negative inverse of the Hessian matrix obtained from numeric optimization of the log posterior.

span.label: empirical Bayes
span.quote: A is an empirical Bayes estimate of the variance of the generating Normal distribution, and S = A gives the scale.

span.label: maximum a posteriori
span.quote: We use the posterior mode, or maximum a posteriori (MAP), as the shrinkage estimator for the coefficient.

span.label: logarithmic fold change - AS ESTIMATED, NOT AS DEFINED. The definition is a ratio of average expression between conditions; the estimate at low counts is `large ... not representative of true differences`. THE SAME SYMBOL NAMES A QUANTITY AND A NUMBER THAT DOES NOT MEASURE IT
span.quote: When the read counts are low or highly variable, the maximum likelihood estimates for the LFCs has high variance, leading to large estimates not representative of true differences, and poor ranking of genes by effect size.

span.label: shrinkage - the family of corrections, and this paper's point is that the family members fail in OPPOSITE directions: a filter loses true signal, a Normal prior flattens true large effects. WHICH ERROR YOU GET IS A CHOICE, AND USUALLY AN UNEXAMINED ONE
span.quote: However, in our analysis, we found that filtering or application of Normal priors each can have drawbacks, either leading to loss of genes with sufficient signal, or overly aggressive shrinkage of true, large LFCs.

span.label: pseudocount - a correction that `must be ADAPTED PER DATASET`. The paper's remedy is to remove the parameter rather than to tune it, which is the same move a field makes when it replaces an inferred name with a measured one
span.quote: One approach is to introduce filtering thresholds and pseudocounts to exclude or moderate estimated LFCs. Filtering may result in a loss of genes from the analysis with true differences in expression, while pseudocounts provide a limited solution that must be adapted per dataset.

span.label: critiques → count filtering as practised in edgeR and limma-voom, which removes genes before analysis and can lose those with sufficient signal
span.quote: The authors of edgeR ( McCarthy et al. , 2012 ) and limma-voom ( Law et al. , 2014 ) suggest using a filtering rule that removes genes with low scaled counts before statistical analysis

span.label: critiques → DESeq2's adaptive Normal prior, which shrinks true large fold changes too aggressively
span.quote: DESeq2 applies an adaptive Normally distributed prior, to produce a shrinkage estimator for the LFC for each gene.

span.label: extends → the empirical Bayes shrinkage tradition itself - the method is offered as a replacement for the prior, not for the framework
span.quote: The proposed method, Approximate Posterior Estimation for generalized linear model, apeglm , has lower bias than previously proposed shrinkage estimators, while still reducing variance for those genes with little information for statistical inference.

span.label: EVERY STANDARD CORRECTION TRADES ONE ERROR FOR THE OPPOSITE ONE: filtering loses genes with sufficient signal, Normal priors over-shrink true large fold changes
span.term: EVERY STANDARD CORRECTION TRADES ONE ERROR FOR THE OPPOSITE ONE: filtering loses genes with sufficient signal, Normal priors over-shrink true large fold changes
span.quote: However, in our analysis, we found that filtering or application of Normal priors each can have drawbacks, either leading to loss of genes with sufficient signal, or overly aggressive shrinkage of true, large LFCs.

span.label: PSEUDOCOUNTS PROVIDE A LIMITED SOLUTION THAT MUST BE ADAPTED PER DATASET - a correction re-tuned per dataset is a free parameter wearing a method's name
span.term: PSEUDOCOUNTS PROVIDE A LIMITED SOLUTION THAT MUST BE ADAPTED PER DATASET - a correction re-tuned per dataset is a free parameter wearing a method's name
span.quote: One approach is to introduce filtering thresholds and pseudocounts to exclude or moderate estimated LFCs. Filtering may result in a loss of genes from the analysis with true differences in expression, while pseudocounts provide a limited solution that must be adapted per dataset.

span.label: SETTING THE THRESHOLD REQUIRES CAREFUL CONSIDERATION OF WHICH GENES MAY BE LOST - the filter is named as a judgement about what to discard, not a setting
span.term: SETTING THE THRESHOLD REQUIRES CAREFUL CONSIDERATION OF WHICH GENES MAY BE LOST - the filter is named as a judgement about what to discard, not a setting
span.quote: Setting the threshold requires careful consideration of which genes may be lost.

span.label: at low or highly variable counts the maximum likelihood LFC has high variance and produces LARGE ESTIMATES NOT REPRESENTATIVE OF TRUE DIFFERENCES - the noise arrives looking like a big effect
span.term: at low or highly variable counts the maximum likelihood LFC has high variance and produces LARGE ESTIMATES NOT REPRESENTATIVE OF TRUE DIFFERENCES - the noise arrives looking like a big effect
span.quote: When the read counts are low or highly variable, the maximum likelihood estimates for the LFCs has high variance, leading to large estimates not representative of true differences, and poor ranking of genes by effect size.

span.label: the proposed heavy-tailed Cauchy prior AVOIDS THE USE OF FILTER THRESHOLDS OR PSEUDOCOUNTS - removing the parameter rather than tuning it
span.term: the proposed heavy-tailed Cauchy prior AVOIDS THE USE OF FILTER THRESHOLDS OR PSEUDOCOUNTS - removing the parameter rather than tuning it
span.quote: Here, we propose the use of a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior distribution for effect sizes, which avoids the use of filter thresholds or pseudocounts.

span.label: the Laplace approximation was consistently more accurate than numerical integration over a grid
span.quote: We also attempted an alternate method for approximating the posterior by integrating the un-normalized posterior over a fine grid, but we found the Laplace approximation was consistently more accurate.

span.label: substituting estimated standard errors for known ones leaves the scale estimate only slightly biased even at very low counts
span.quote: We found that the resulting estimate of A is only slightly biased, even when counts are very low ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ).

span.label: shrinkage improves the ranking of genes by effect size relative to methods that do not shrink at all
span.quote: We also show that apeglm shrunken estimates improve gene rankings by LFCs, relative to methods which do not apply Bayesian shrinkage on the LFCs. apeglm is available as an open-source R package on Bioconductor, and can be easily called from within the DESeq2 software. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 NB model for RNA-seq counts We start with summarized measures of gene expression for the experiment, represented by a matrix of read or fragment counts.

span.label: the difference between conditions, defined as the log ratio of average expression levels
span.quote: The difference is usually defined in terms of the logarithmic fold change (LFC) between average expression levels of different conditions.

span.label: the local false sign rate given as a two-case posterior probability keyed on the sign of the MAP estimate
span.quote: Following Stephens (2017) , the local FSR is defined as the posterior probability that the posterior mode (MAP) is of the false sign, that is for gene g , lfsr g = { p ( β g k < 0 ) MAP of β g k ≥ 0 p ( β g k ≥ 0 ) MAP of β g k < 0.

span.label: the negative binomial model with its mean decomposed into a scaling factor and an expression quantity
span.quote: The mean μ gi is a product of a scaling factor s gi and a quantity q gi that is proportional to the expression level of the gene g .

span.label: maximum likelihood
span.quote: When the read counts are low or highly variable, the maximum likelihood estimates for the LFCs has high variance, leading to large estimates not representative of true differences, and poor ranking of genes by effect size.

span.label: variance
span.quote: When the read counts are low or highly variable, the maximum likelihood estimates for the LFCs has high variance, leading to large estimates not representative of true differences, and poor ranking of genes by effect size.

span.label: posterior SD
span.quote: Providing low variance posterior mode effect sizes and their posterior SD allows for various downstream uses, for example, plotting LFC estimates from two experiments against each other in a scatter plot, without having to make arbitrary filtering

span.label: library size
span.quote: The expression level of a gene in an RNA-Seq experiment is proportional across samples to a scaled count, representing the number of observed single- or paired-end reads that could be assigned to a given gene at a given library size.

span.label: runtimes for the pipeline on a ten-thousand-gene simulation - dispersion and MLE fitting, Normal-prior shrinkage, Cauchy-prior shrinkage, and MAP-only
span.quote: Running apeglm is efficient: for the simulation dataset modeled on the Pickrell data (10 000 genes and 5 versus 5 samples), running DESeq2 to obtain dispersion estimates and MLE coefficients takes 4.7 s on a laptop with one core, running LFC shrinkage with the DESeq2 Normal prior takes 2.9 s, and running LFC shrinkage with the apeglm Cauchy prior takes 4.1 s.
